presentingComplaint: Sudden onset of multiple episodes of bright red to maroon-coloured blood mixed with stool over the past 6 hours, associated with lightheadedness.
history: 68-year-old man with known colonic diverticulosis (diagnosed on colonoscopy 3 years ago) and hypertension on amlodipine presents with acute onset of painless haematochezia - five large-volume bowel movements of maroon stool with clots since this morning, no preceding severe abdominal pain. He denies haematemesis, melena, or NSAID/aspirin use in the preceding week, though he takes low-dose aspirin for cardiovascular prophylaxis. No fevers, no recent travel, no alcohol excess, no known liver disease. He felt dizzy on standing and had one presyncopal episode at home prompting his wife to bring him to the emergency department. No prior variceal bleeding or cirrhosis. Bowel habit was normal until today.
examination: Pale conjunctivae. Mildly anxious, oriented. Abdomen soft, non-tender, no distension, no peritonism, no palpable mass. Digital rectal exam reveals maroon-coloured stool with clots, no external haemorrhoids seen, no anal fissure. No stigmata of chronic liver disease (no spider naevi, no palmar erythema, no caput medusae). Cardiovascular exam: tachycardic, no murmurs. Postural drop in blood pressure noted on standing.
imaging: CT angiography abdomen/pelvis: active contrast extravasation into a sigmoid colon diverticulum, no evidence of bowel wall thickening or perforation

Colonoscopy (after bowel prep, once stabilized): extensive sigmoid diverticulosis with a single diverticulum showing a visible vessel and adherent clot, no active spurting at time of scope; no colitis, no mass lesion
differentialDiagnoses: Upper GI bleed with rapid transit (brisk haematochezia)
finalDiagnosis: Acute lower gastrointestinal bleeding due to colonic diverticular haemorrhage
citations: ACG Clinical Guideline: Management of Patients with Acute Lower Gastrointestinal Bleeding 2016
contraindications: Avoid resuming aspirin/antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy until bleeding source controlled and haemodynamically stable
Bowel preparation for colonoscopy should be given once patient is hemodynamically resuscitated
edgeCases: Up to 15% of presumed lower GI bleeds are actually brisk upper GI bleeds presenting as haematochezia - upper endoscopy should be considered if NG aspirate is bloody or if hemodynamic instability is disproportionate, or if colonoscopy is non-diagnostic
Diverticular bleeding is often self-limited (stops spontaneously in ~75-80% of cases) but has a rebleed rate of up to 25-40%
